newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech cen bank finally intervenes to support crown.
newsitem.headline: Czech cen bank finally intervenes to support crown.

text.p: The Czech National Bank (CNB) made clear it was serious about defending the crown with market interventions after the currency fell to what traders believe was the central bank's support level.
After warning the market for months it would not allow the crown to fall too much, the central bank stepped in with two rounds of intervention and vowed to continue buying crowns if necessary.

The crown lost about one full percentage point in early Thursday trading to hit a record low of 5.00 percent against its dollar/mark basket parity. Following the intervention it rebounded to minus 3.4 percent.
"The CNB today intervened on the forex market with the aim of stabilising the crown's exchange rate," a CNB statement said. "If needed, the CNB is ready for further intervention," it added.
The statement added the crown's fall was due to fluctuations of several foreign currencies.
It did not elaborate, but some traders said foreign investors were getting nervous over some emerging market economies troubled by weak external position, such as Thailand.
The CNB did not reveal the amounts it had spent on reviving the crown, but analysts estimated it cost several millions of dollars in total.
At the end of March, the CNB's foreign exchange reserves were almost unchanged from the month before at $11.7 billion.
The CNB then fixed the crown 3.4 percent weaker against the basket midpoint. In mid-afternoon activity, the crown remained steady at -3.3 percent.

Tomas Novak, a dealer at bank CSOB, told Reuters the central bank first entered the market at about 0730 GMT on Thursday, but after failing to create a strong change in market sentiment, re-entered to give the crown a further boost.
"At first they were trying with small amounts and now they are continuing with larger amounts," he said during the operation.

The central bank has been threatening to act since February when the crown -- boosted by demand from a wave of nearly 50 billion crowns worth of crown-denominated Eurobond issues -- hit a record high of 5.51 percent on the appreciation side of basket parity.

Since then the crown has fallen sharply driven by worries about the country's overall macroeconomic prospects and a widespread belief that the CNB would heed government calls for a relaxation of monetary policy to boost growth.

But Thursday marked the first time it had actually entered the market to move the crown since February 1996 when the band within which the crown is fixed was widened to +/-7.5 percent from a previous +/-0.5 percent.
Analysts said it appeared as though the long-rumoured, but never confirmed, five percent internal band at the central bank -- which if touched would trigger intervention -- had been confirmed.
They added that while the central bank moves would have a short-term effect on the market, further action was needed to stop the crown from weakening again.
"The five percent band appears to be real," said one Frankfurt analyst.

"(But) I think the market feels that intervention by itself will not be able to sustain the sentiment. Reserves are not that high, so the market overall is still bearish about the currency," he added.
